thread.title: Juicy Dividend Payers Come Under Attack - My Wide Moat 7

author: Dale Roberts
title: Juicy Dividend Payers Come Under Attack - My Wide Moat 7
text:
There have been some overnight rate increases in the US and in Canada. Now certainly the US has been more aggressive as there is the perception or truth that the economy is more robust and might need a little cooling off. Canada appears to trudge along not doing much but offering a much greater earnings yield compared to the major US indices. I wrote about that possibility in this article Why Canadian Markets May Outperform US Markets, Again.
And on that front, yes, the Canadian broad based indices have started to move higher relative to the US markets. From yahoofinance here's the 3 month chart comparing the Canadian TSX 60 ETF to the S&P 500 index benchmark. We see the Canadian index, in lighter blue, attempt to pull away with some true vigor in May, only or recede, but still does provide some outperformance for the period at 8.5% vs. 6.4%. Of course, past performance does not guarantee future returns.
And given the rate increases the higher yielding companies have come under price pressure. Here's the recent US rate history.
While Canada has been more subdued.
The rate increases in Canada and the US have put pressure on those higher yielders. Canadian investors will also react in anticipation of higher rates in response to the US moves. All said, the rate increases are out of our control, the actions of other investors are out of our control. Investors should concentrate on what they can control, important issues such as asset allocation and costs and sticking to that investment plan. If we start reacting and guessing, well bad things can happen. Emotion combined with guess work is not a good combination that will lead to sensible investment decisions.
Now back to my Canadian Wide Moat 7 and the 'beating' it's taking. From that original article -
Canadian banking is dominated by the Big 5: Royal Bank of Canada (NYSE: RY ), Toronto Dominion Bank (NYSE: TD ), Scotiabank (NYSE: BNS ), CIBC (NYSE: CM ) and Bank of Montreal (NYSE: BMO ).
The Telco space is dominated by the Big 3: Bell Canada (NYSE: BCE ), Telus (NYSE: TU ) and Rogers (NYSE: RCI ).
Canada's two big pipelines are Enbridge (NYSE: ENB ) and TransCanada Pipelines (NYSE: TRP ).
For my Wide Moat 7 I hold RY, TD, BNS, BCE, TU, ENB and TRP. Not all of the companies have taken large price hits, it is more concentrated in the pipelines that also face regulatory uncertainties. But my Wide Moat 7 has walked right into it, as Telcos and Banks and Utilities are known to react negatively in the short term to interest rate increases. That said, here's an interesting article from Leon Frazer that shows that over the longer term and in a rising rate environment those sectors are not adversely affected. Over the longer term, once again, business success will do the talking.
Enbridge, of course, is in the midst of a massive acquisition and the market simply does not know how to digest it all. The market has also fallen out of love with BCE. Here's a year over year look from July of 2017 to end of June 2018. Portfolio 1 in Enbridge, Portfolio 2 is TransCanada and Portfolio 3 is Bell Canada. For the period the Vanguard High Dividend Yield Index Delivered 5.76%. These are laggards and then some.
But given that these are higher yielding companies, most or much of the value delivered to an investor comes by way of those Big Juicy Dividends. So while certainly under price pressure, the dividend pressure? not so much. Here's the dividend history back to 2014, once again compared to the Vanguard Index. The Dividends are reinvested. And once again, the rationale for buying the Wide Moat 7 is for that dividend stability which of course always comes back to business success over longer periods, hopefully protected by those wide moats. Mission accomplished on that front. All 7 companies are continuing with their dividend growth plans. Even Enbridge has publicly declared that they will raise their dividend by 10% annual over the next 3 years or more. Portfolio 1 is the Wide Moat 7. Portfolio 2 is the Vanguard High Dividend Yield index.
Those decent price drops allowed me to load up on even more juicier dividend yields at time of purchase. As my readers know, for my US stocks holdings, I bought 'em 'without looking' and I have added to them without looking. I have simply repurchased the laggards in an attempt to rebalance the portfolio on the fly. The same holds true for the Canadian holdings. I have simply repurchased (reinvested in) those companies without any evaluation, and the companies that were under greater distress received greater funds for reinvestment. I was able to buy the Bell's, TransCanada's and Enbridge's at yields well over 5% up to hear 6.5%. For now, those yields are in the books and the dividends will be harvested as I have entered my new work/life stage that you might call semi-retirement. I left my fulltime work and now write on Seeking Alpha and cutthecrapinvesting.com. I will also be writing for some of the lower fee investment houses in Canada.
While I bought my Wide Moat 7 largely for those dividends, I would also of course appreciates some capital appreciation. On that front, I am more likely to be rewarded with the big Canadians banks as they are the North American large cap subsector that has even beat the pants off of Warren Buffett, perhaps we could say they have beat Mr. B at his own wide moat game.
At times we are rewarded on that front for investing when companies are truly in the dog house. Here's a look at those 3 companies in price terms. BCE is essentially flat over the last 3 months, but we see that the two pipes are threatening to recover in price terms. From google finance.
On the repurchasing without looking file, I am also being rewarded with some higher prices on CVS and QCOM . Yes, those are very short term moves, but perhaps that is the start of some market comfort for these companies. Over the longer term I have been rewarded for my patience and trust in NKE and WMT and UTX and LOW . I added to these companies when they were out of favor. All of these names have made more pronounced and longer term advances. I will of course follow up on the index skimming exercise known as my Dividend Aristocrat 15.
On the US side of the juicy dividend file, many investors have witnessed the price declines in the US telco oligopoly list of Verizon ( VZ ), AT & T ( T ), Sprint ( S ) and T-Mobile ( TMUS ). Will investors who have demonstrated patience with that grouping be rewarded over time with the juicy dividends and perhaps some nice capital appreciation? Only time will tell, and I will track that event and follow up with future articles. Once again, I'd be on the side that if you hold 'em, buy 'em, stick with 'em. That's assuming of course that you currently hold a sensible well balanced portfolio and you bought those companies for 'good reasons'.
We'll see how that works out for my Canadians holdings and this US telco grouping.
Author's note: Thanks for reading. Please always know and invest within your risk tolerance level. Always know all tax implications and consequences. If you liked this article, please hit that "Like" button. If you'd like notices of future articles, click the "Follow" button.
Happy Investing.
Dale
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, NKE, BCE, TU, ENB, TRP, CVS, WBA, MSFT, MMM, CL, JNJ, QCOM, MDT, BRK.B, ABT, PEP, TXN, WMT, UTX, LOW, BNS.
